t: Connected vehicles: sensing, identity and trust
d: Cars are rolling sensor platforms. This line of work asks what their data can reveal, who is driving, and how to catch the signals that put everyone on the road at risk.

t: Hybrid quantum-classical intrusion detection
d: Can a small quantum circuit, paired with classical deep learning, help catch network attacks and mobile malware? We built one framework that does both.

t: IoT device identity and network incidents
d: A network that cannot tell which device sent a packet, or whether that device was tampered with, cannot defend itself. We identify devices and attacks from packet headers alone.

t: Acoustic side channels on phones
d: A phone lying behind your keyboard can hear which keys you press. We showed how, with no training data and no language model, which means it works on random passwords too.

t: Explainable and applied AI
d: The methods behind my security work also answer questions in food safety, public safety, language and the workplace, with an emphasis on explaining why a model decides what it does.

t: Extending what a car can see and sense
d: A car's own sensors stop at the truck in front of it, and the phone in the cabin knows more about the road than it seems. This work shares views between vehicles and turns phone and car sensors into a picture of the road.

t: Scoring and coaching drivers from in-vehicle data
d: The same in-vehicle data that identifies a driver can also score how they drive, as they drive, and turn that score into feedback people act on.

t: Quantum machine learning for Raman spectroscopy
d: Hybrid quantum-classical models are not only for network traffic. Raman spectra, the light fingerprints of molecules, are a natural test bed: one-dimensional, noisy and costly to label.

t: Sharing spectrum fairly: fractional frequency reuse
d: Before security, I worked on how cellular networks share spectrum. My M.S. thesis at Bilkent asked how to split a cell's subcarriers between users near the base station and users at the edge, so the network is both fast and fair.

t: Catching GNSS spoofing with the car's own sensors
d: Can a car notice that its GPS is lying, using only the data it already has? This project builds a lightweight spoofing detector from the vehicle's own motion data.

t: Leak-free benchmarks for IoT traffic classifiers
d: Many intrusion-detection and device-fingerprinting papers report near-perfect accuracy. This project measures how much of it survives once shortcuts in the data are removed.

t: Does a quantum layer really help? Honest benchmarks for quantum intrusion detection
d: Hybrid quantum-classical models have reported strong intrusion-detection results in simulation. This project asks which part of that comes from the quantum layer, and what survives on real quantum hardware.

t: Explanations you can check: explainable intrusion and malware detection
d: Security analysts are asked to act on alerts from models they cannot see inside. This project tests whether today's explanation methods tell them the truth about why a detector fired, and builds explanations an analyst can check.

t: Spotting intruders on the car's internal network
d: Inside every car, dozens of computers talk over one shared bus with no sender authentication. This project builds detectors that notice when a message on that bus does not belong there.

t: Do earbuds, smart speakers and video calls leak what you type?
d: We showed in 2015 that one phone can tell which keys you press from their sound. Microphones are now in earbuds, speakers and every video call. This project measures how much they leak, and what stops it.

t: Attacking and defending a campus chatbot
d: Chatbots that answer from a university's own pages are spreading fast. This project red-teams one: can a planted page or a crafted question make it give wrong or harmful answers, and which defenses hold up?

t: Intrusion detection that fits on the device
d: Most IoT devices cannot run a full intrusion detector. This project shrinks detectors until they run on a microcontroller, and measures what accuracy that costs.

t: Is the Internet of Things ready for post-quantum cryptography?
d: NIST published its first post-quantum cryptography standards in 2024. This project measures what moving to them costs on small IoT devices, and whether it quietly breaks the security tools that watch their traffic.

t: Tamper-evident identity for IoT devices on a blockchain
d: A network should know which devices are allowed on it and notice when one is cloned or tampered with. This project records device identities on a permissioned blockchain and checks live traffic against them.

t: Naming the app without reading the traffic
d: Encryption hides what is inside a packet, but not its size, its timing or its direction. This project asks how much that metadata reveals, how to use it to manage and secure networks without decrypting anything, and how to protect users from the same leak.

t: Catching ghost vehicles in V2X messages
d: Connected cars broadcast their position and speed many times a second, and other cars act on those messages. This project detects messages that describe cars that are not there.

t: Training intrusion detectors without pooling the data
d: Every gateway sees different traffic, and most cannot share it. This project trains a shared intrusion detector across many sites while the data stays where it was collected, and asks what happens when one of those sites is malicious.

t: Can an attacker slip past the intrusion detector?
d: Machine-learning detectors can be fooled by small changes to their input. For network traffic, the attacker cannot change just anything: packets must stay valid and the attack must still work. This project measures how robust detectors really are against attackers who play by those rules.

t: Telling radios apart by their imperfections
d: No two radios are built exactly alike. Tiny flaws in each transmitter leave a signature in every signal it sends. This project asks whether those signatures can identify IoT devices reliably, even as the radio moves and conditions change.

t: Sharing car data without giving away where you have been
d: Connected cars share their position to make traffic maps and safety services work. A handful of those points can reveal where a driver lives and works. This project measures that risk and tests protections that keep the shared data useful.

t: Securing the EV charging network
d: Electric-vehicle chargers are networked computers connected to the power grid. If an attacker controls many of them at once, switching them together could stress the local grid. This project studies those attacks and how to detect them early.

t: Can a language model help triage security alerts?
d: Security teams face far more alerts than they can read, and most turn out to be harmless. This project tests whether a language model that reads the context around each alert can put the real incidents first, and how to catch it when it gets the facts wrong.
